Boeing's 2023 10-K gives four percentages for union representation as of December 31, 2023: one overall figure and three for individual unions.

| Percentage | What it refers to |
|---|---|
| **33%** | All union-represented employees together: about 57,000 people out of a total workforce of about 171,000, covered by collective bargaining agreements. |
| **21%** | International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers (IAM). This covers two major agreements: IAM District 751 in Washington (expires September 2024) and IAM District 837 in Missouri (expires July 2025). |
| **10%** | Society of Professional Engineering Employees in Aerospace (SPEEA). This covers two major agreements, SPEEA Professional and SPEEA Technical, both expiring October 2026. |
| **1%** | United Automobile, Aerospace and Agricultural Implement Workers of America (UAW). This covers one major agreement, UAW District 1069 in Pennsylvania (expires April 2027). |

The 33% figure comes from the Risk Factors section (10-K page 9). The three union figures come from the Human Capital table (10-K page 2).

The three named unions add up to 32%, one point short of the 33% total. The filing doesn't explain the gap. It may be the other unions Boeing deals with (it says it works with 10 U.S. and 4 non-U.S. labor organizations), rounding, or both.

Apple's fiscal 2024 Form 10-K says weaker foreign currencies hurt four results compared with fiscal 2023. All four are in the Management's Discussion and Analysis section.

**Net sales in three regions (page 22)**
1. **Greater China:** A weaker renminbi against the dollar hurt sales compared with the prior year. Net sales fell 8%, to $66.95 billion from $72.56 billion. The main reason was lower iPhone and iPad sales.
2. **Japan:** A weaker yen hurt sales. Net sales still rose 3%, to $25.05 billion from $24.26 billion, mainly because iPhone sales were higher.
3. **Rest of Asia Pacific:** Weaker foreign currencies had a "net unfavorable" effect. Net sales still rose 4%, to $30.66 billion from $29.62 billion, mainly because Services sales were higher.

**Products gross margin (page 24)**
4. Products gross margin rose to $109.63 billion from $108.80 billion, and its percentage rose to 37.2% from 36.5%. Cost savings drove the increase. A different mix of products and weaker foreign currencies against the dollar partly offset it.

**Things to keep in mind:**
- The filing doesn't give a dollar amount for any of these currency effects.
- It doesn't mention currency for Americas or Europe sales, Services gross margin, sales by product category, or operating expenses.
- The risk factors and market-risk sections say in general terms that a stronger dollar hurts net sales and gross margins. They don't link any other 2024 result to currency.

Apple's 10-K ties these matters to four points in calendar 2025: three exact days and one month. Two of the developments happened on April 23.

**April 23, 2025: EU Digital Markets Act investigations** (Item 3, Legal Proceedings, p. 18)
- **Article 5(4) investigation:** The European Commission fined Apple €500 million. It also ordered Apple to remove the technical and commercial restrictions that stop developers from steering users to distribution channels outside the App Store. Apple has appealed.
- **Article 6(4) investigation:** The same day, the Commission issued preliminary findings on whether Apple's new contract terms for third-party app developers and app marketplaces break the DMA. If the Commission finds a violation, it can order Apple to stop and fine it up to 10% of annual worldwide net sales.

**April 30, 2025: Epic Games, U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California** (Item 3, p. 18)
- The court found Apple in violation of its 2021 Injunction. It barred Apple from:
  - charging any commission or fee on purchases made outside an app
  - limiting how developers direct consumers to those purchases
  - otherwise interfering with a consumer's choice to buy inside or outside an app
- It denied Apple's motion to narrow or vacate the 2021 Injunction.
- It referred Apple to the U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of California to decide whether criminal contempt proceedings are appropriate.

**September 2, 2025: Google search antitrust case, U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia** (Item 1A, Risk Factors, p. 14)
- The court ordered remedies following its August 5, 2024 finding that Google broke U.S. antitrust laws. This matters to Apple because Google pays it to offer Google search on Apple's platforms.
- The filing doesn't say what the remedies are. It notes that the court may still change them and that both the DOJ and Google can appeal.
- If the order is reversed on appeal, remedies the DOJ originally proposed could be imposed. One example is barring Google from offering Apple commercial terms for search distribution.

**October 2025 (month only): Epic Games appeal, Ninth Circuit** (Item 3, p. 18)
- The court heard oral arguments in Apple's fast-tracked appeal of the April 30 ruling.

**Mentioned without a day or month:**
- Apple's appeal of the Article 5(4) decision
- Apple's appeal of the April 30 ruling
- The denial of Apple's request to pause that ruling during the appeal (the filing doesn't say which court denied it)
- Settlements of "certain matters" in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2025, which Apple says weren't material

Other events in these sections are dated before 2025, so I left them out. These include the EU investigations opened on March 25 and June 24, 2024, the DOJ lawsuit filed on March 21, 2024, and the September 10, 2024 European Court of Justice ruling against Apple in the Irish tax (State Aid) case.

Apple's fiscal 2025 10-K gives six percentages that fit your criteria: two for fiscal 2025 net sales and four for receivables as of September 27, 2025.

**Net sales, fiscal 2025** (Item 1, "Markets and Distribution," PDF page 5)

- **40%**: the share of total net sales made through Apple's direct channels, such as its retail and online stores and its direct sales force.
- **60%**: the share of total net sales made through indirect channels, such as third-party cellular network carriers and other resellers.

Together, these two cover all of Apple's net sales.

**Receivables, as of September 27, 2025** (Note 4, "Accounts Receivable," PDF page 42)

Trade receivables are amounts customers owe Apple.
- **12%**: the share of total trade receivables owed by one customer, the only customer at 10% or more. The filing doesn't name it.
- **34%**: the share of total trade receivables owed by third-party cellular network carriers as a group.

The filing doesn't say whether the 12% customer is a carrier. The two figures could overlap, so they shouldn't be added together.

Vendor non-trade receivables are a separate category. They're amounts owed by manufacturing vendors that buy components from Apple to build parts or assemble finished products for it. Apple doesn't count these component sales as net sales.
- **46% and 23%**: each figure is one vendor's share of total vendor non-trade receivables. These are the only two vendors at 10% or more, and neither is named.

**What I left out**
- **Earlier-period figures:** the carriers' 38% and the two vendors' 44% and 23%, all as of September 28, 2024.
- **Disclosure thresholds:** the "10% or more" cutoffs, which only decide which customers and vendors are reported.

I found four dividend amounts for the 6.00% Series A Mandatory Convertible Preferred Stock in the main body of Boeing's 2024 10-K:

| Amount | What it represents | Where it appears (printed page) |
|---|---|---|
| Up to $345 million per year | The cash Boeing expects to need each year to pay dividends on the preferred shares until they must convert to common stock on October 15, 2027. | Item 1A, Risk Factors, liquidity risk (p. 17) |
| $58 million | Dividends that built up in 2024, from the October 31, 2024 issue date to year-end. Boeing subtracts this from the $11,817 million net loss attributable to Boeing shareholders. That gives the $11,875 million net loss attributable to common shareholders, which is used for loss per share. | Statement of Operations (p. 54), Summary of Business Segment Data (p. 59), Note 4 on earnings per share (p. 73) |
| $72 million | Dividends declared in December 2024 for holders of record on January 1, 2025, and paid in cash on January 15, 2025. The equity statement shows this as a reduction to retained earnings. | Statement of Equity (p. 58), Note 19 on shareholders' equity (p. 106) |
| $12.50 per share | The per-share amount of the $72 million dividend. | Note 19 (p. 106) |

**How the $58 million and $72 million fit together (my calculation, not stated in the filing):** The $72 million covers the whole first dividend period, October 31, 2024 to January 15, 2025, which runs into 2025. That works out to 5.75 million shares × $12.50 ≈ $72 million. About 60 of the period's 75 days fall in 2024, which gives roughly $58 million. The $345 million also equals 5.75 million shares × $60 per share per year.

**Left out, as you asked:** Exhibit 4.1 also gives $60.00 per share per year and $15.00 per share for each full quarter.

NVIDIA's fiscal 2025 10-K gives one combined figure for gains and losses on equity securities and five figures for parts of it. All of them are recorded in Other income (expense), net.

| FY2025 amount | What it represents | Source |
|---|---|---|
| **$1,030M net gain** | Total net gains on non-marketable and publicly-held equity securities combined. The cash flow statement shows it as $(1,030)M, because this non-cash gain is subtracted from net income to get operating cash flow. | Cash flow statement, p. 56 |
| **$163M** | Net unrealized gains on publicly-held shares NVIDIA still held at year-end. This is the gain for fiscal 2025 alone, not a running total, so it isn't one of the cumulative amounts you excluded. | Note 7, p. 66 |
| **$88M** | Net realized gains on publicly-held shares sold during the year. It equals sale proceeds minus the shares' value at the start of the year (or the purchase price, if bought during the year). So it only counts fiscal 2025 gains, not gains since NVIDIA first bought the shares. | Note 7, p. 66 |
| **$816M** | Unrealized gains on non-marketable (private company) investments. These are increases in their recorded value, based on observable prices in orderly transactions for the same or similar securities of the same company. | Note 8, p. 69 |

**Subtotals I calculated (the filing doesn't state these):**
- Publicly-held securities: $163M + $88M = $251M net gain
- Non-marketable securities: $816M − $59M = $757M net gain
- Together that's $1,008M, which is $22M less than the $1,030M total. The filing doesn't explain the gap. It also gives no separate figure for realized gains or losses on non-marketable securities sold, even though NVIDIA received $171M from such sales in fiscal 2025.

I found five effects in NVIDIA's fiscal 2023 10-K that it describes as having happened or possibly having happened. They appear in the risk factor on laws and regulations (p. 28) and in the "Russia" part of management's discussion (p. 37).

1. **Blocked access to Russia, Belarus and parts of Ukraine.** The sanctions and export controls that the U.S. and other jurisdictions imposed in response to the war blocked NVIDIA's products, services and support from entering Russia, Belarus and certain regions of Ukraine.
2. **Direct sales to Russia stopped.** NVIDIA stopped selling directly to Russia in fiscal 2023.
3. **Russian operations closed.** Later in fiscal 2023, NVIDIA closed its business operations in Russia.
4. **EMEA end-customer sales affected.** The filing says the war "has impacted end customer sales in EMEA."
5. **Partner revenue possibly hurt.** NVIDIA's revenue from partners that sell into Russia "may have been negatively impacted" by the war. This is the only effect the filing says may have happened rather than stating it did.

The filing doesn't give a dollar amount for any of these effects. The only size it offers is that direct sales to Russia in fiscal 2022 were immaterial.

**What I left out:**
- **Future EMEA impact:** the statement that the EMEA impact "may continue to do so in the future." That's a future risk.
- **U.S. license rules from Q3 fiscal 2023:** these cover exports of A100 and H100 products to China and Russia. The filing says they target China's chip and supercomputing industries and doesn't link them to the war.
- **General risk language:** statements about war, sanctions or cyber-attacks that don't mention Ukraine.

NVIDIA's fiscal 2026 10-K gives five goodwill amounts that fit what you asked for: three balances at January 25, 2026 and two amounts added during the year. The Groq deal accounts for $14.4 billion of the $15.6 billion added. The filing doesn't say where the other $1.2 billion or so came from.

**Balances at January 25, 2026**

- **$20.8 billion ($20,832 million on the balance sheet):** All goodwill on the books. NVIDIA's yearly impairment check in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026 found no impairment.
- **$20.5 billion:** The part assigned to the Compute & Networking unit.
- **$370 million:** The part assigned to the Graphics unit. None of the fiscal 2026 additions went to this unit.

**Added during fiscal 2026**

- **$15.6 billion:** All goodwill added during the year, all of it assigned to Compute & Networking.
- **$14.4 billion:** Goodwill from the Groq deal in December 2025. NVIDIA got a non-exclusive license to Groq's language processing unit technology and hired some Groq employees. It didn't buy any customer contracts, products or ownership stake. The filing says this goodwill mainly reflects the hired staff and future development of the licensed technology. It's assigned to Compute & Networking and is tax-deductible. The deal also created a separate $2.5 billion technology asset, which will be written off over five years. NVIDIA paid $13.0 billion at closing and owes $4 billion more within one year (that figure includes imputed interest).

**The unexplained $1.2 billion**

The $15.6 billion total minus Groq's $14.4 billion leaves about $1.2 billion. The filing doesn't explain this amount. My guess is that it came from other acquisitions, but the 10-K doesn't say so. The cash flow statement shows $1,535 million spent on "acquisitions, net of cash acquired," and the filing mentions buying a company on December 15, 2025.

Sources: Note 5 (p. 63), Note 2 (p. 61), balance sheet (p. 53), cash flow statement (p. 55), Item 5 (p. 34).

JPMorgan's 2023 10-K gives six amounts for the effect of adopting the TDR guidance. All were recorded on January 1, 2023 using the "modified retrospective" method. That means they went straight to opening balances and retained earnings, not through the provision for credit losses or net income. Page numbers below are the 10-K's printed pages.

| Amount ($ millions) | What it measures | Where |
|---|---|---|
| **587 decrease** | The Firm's total net decrease in its allowance for credit losses, before tax. It came from moving most loans modified for borrowers in financial difficulty off a discounted-cash-flow, loan-by-loan method and onto a pooled ("portfolio-based") method. The Firm says this was mainly driven by residential real estate and credit card. All of it was in the allowance for loan losses, and the MD&A also describes it as a $587 million reduction in that allowance. | Note 1 (p. 173); Note 13 (pp. 256, 258, 260); MD&A (pp. 58, 131–132) |
| **489 decrease** | The consumer, excluding credit card portfolio's share of the $587 million, shown as "cumulative effect of a change in accounting principle" in the allowance for loan losses table | pp. 132, 258 |
| **100 decrease** | The credit card portfolio's share | pp. 132, 258 |
| **2 increase** | The wholesale portfolio's share, a small offset | pp. 132, 258 |
| **591 decrease** | The decrease in the Consumer & Community Banking (CCB) segment's allowance for loan losses, driven by residential real estate and credit card | CCB selected metrics, footnote (g), p. 70 |
| **446 increase** | The after-tax increase to retained earnings at January 1, 2023 | Note 1 (p. 173); Note 13 (p. 256) |

Things to watch:
- **$449 million is not the TDR-only figure.** The statement of changes in stockholders' equity (p. 169) shows $449 million under "cumulative effect of change in accounting principles" in retained earnings. That line combines the TDR guidance with a hedge accounting standard adopted the same day. The filing calls the hedging change's effect on retained earnings "not material," so the roughly $3 million difference is probably that.
- **Before tax vs. after tax.** By my own subtraction, the $141 million gap between $587 million and $446 million is probably the tax effect. The filing doesn't state the tax amount.
- **CCB vs. the Firm.** The filing doesn't explain why the CCB decrease ($591 million) is $4 million larger than the Firm's ($587 million). That implies small net increases in other segments, which aren't broken out.
- **Lending commitments weren't affected.** The allowance for lending-related commitments shows no adjustment. So for this adoption, the credit loss and loan loss figures are the same.

Pfizer explains the change in a footnote to its intangible assets table (Note 10A). It says the rise from $18,893 million to $21,760 million "primarily reflects $8.0 billion for the acquisition of Metsera." Two things partly offset that: $3.9 billion of IPR&D impairments, and two assets moving out of IPR&D into developed technology rights.

**The increase: buying Metsera.** Pfizer bought Metsera on November 13, 2025. Metsera is a clinical-stage company developing obesity and cardiometabolic medicines. Pfizer paid $65.60 per share in cash, plus up to $20.65 per share more if three milestones are met. The total consideration had a fair value of $8.0 billion. Pfizer recorded $8.0 billion of intangible assets from the deal, all of it IPR&D, plus $2.2 billion of goodwill (Note 2A). These amounts are provisional because the purchase accounting isn't finished, so they could change. Two Metsera programs, the MET-097i+MET-233i combination and MET-097i on its own, are now among the largest IPR&D assets.

**The main offset: impairments.** IPR&D impairments in 2025 came to $3,903 million, part of $4.94 billion in total intangible asset impairments. Pfizer gives one reason for all of these charges: they were "primarily due to changes in development plans and updated long-range commercial forecasts" (Note 4). The biggest IPR&D write-downs were:
- $1.6 billion for disitamab vedotin
- $820 million for Tukysa (tucatinib)
- $820 million for osivelotor

The impaired assets were written down to an estimated fair value of $4.4 billion, using a discounted cash flow model. The key inputs were:
- expected cash flows and their timing, including competitive, legal and regulatory pressures
- the probability that ongoing trials succeed technically and win approval
- the discount rate and tax rate

The filing doesn't give a separate reason for each asset's 2025 charge. Some related facts appear elsewhere in it, though Pfizer doesn't link them to these charges:
- Tukysa and disitamab vedotin were already written down in 2024, by $400 million and $200 million, "reflecting emerging competition."
- Osivelotor was put on a partial FDA clinical hold in December 2024. New enrollment is expected to restart in early 2026.

**The second offset: transfers after approval.** $600 million for Padcev and $590 million for talazoparib (Talzenna) moved from IPR&D to developed technology rights. This is a reclassification, not a loss. Under Pfizer's policy, an IPR&D asset isn't amortized until it is approved in a major market. At that point it is reclassified and starts amortizing. A program that is abandoned is written off as an impairment instead.

**Putting it together.** The named items ($8.0 billion − $3.9 billion − $1.19 billion ≈ $2.9 billion) account for almost all of the $2.87 billion net increase. Pfizer says "primarily" and doesn't explain the small remainder. Pfizer's big 2025 licensing deals didn't add to this balance, because the IPR&D asset only includes projects gained by acquiring companies. **The other four don't qualify:**
- **NVIDIA:** Goodwill rose $758 million from acquisitions, and NVIDIA issued shares to "key employees of a company we acquired." The filing never names the company. Its only named deal is the Arm purchase, which was cancelled in 2022.
- **Apple:** The filing names no acquired company. It only says in general terms that Apple buys third-party businesses and technology.
- **JPMorgan Chase:** The Apple Card deal is a commitment to buy a credit card portfolio, which is assets rather than a company, and it isn't expected to close for about 24 months. The goodwill note shows no business acquisitions in 2025. First Republic was bought in 2023, and only some of its assets and liabilities.
- **ExxonMobil:** In 2025 it bought "key technology and assets from Superior Graphite," not the company itself. Its company acquisitions were Pioneer in 2024 and Denbury in 2023.

Berkshire also bought OxyChem, Occidental's chemicals business, but that closed on January 2, 2026, after the fiscal year ended. Pfizer's 2025 deals with 3SBio and YaoPharma were drug licensing agreements, not acquisitions.

**Two of the eight filings qualify: Walmart's (JD.com) and Pfizer's (Haleon).**

**Walmart, fiscal 2025 10-K: JD.com.** In August 2024, Walmart "sold its investment in JD.com." It got about $3.6 billion in net proceeds and booked a $0.3 billion realized loss (Note 8, p. 70). The filing calls this a sale of the whole investment. It also says the sale was the main reason the value of Walmart's equity investments fell $4.2 billion that year.

**Pfizer, 2025 10-K: Haleon.** Pfizer had sold part of its Haleon stake in 2024 and still owned about 15% at year-end 2024. In the first quarter of 2025 it "sold the remaining portion of our investment in Haleon" for $6.3 billion, with a net loss of $144 million (Note 2C, p. 66; MD&A, p. 48).

**Why the other six don't qualify:**
- **NVIDIA:** It reports $88 million of realized gains on publicly held stocks it sold and $171 million from selling private-company stakes. It doesn't name any of the companies.
- **Apple:** It doesn't disclose selling a stake in any named company.
- **JPMorgan Chase:** It still holds about 18.6 million Visa Class B-2 shares. Its 2025 First Republic gain came from a settlement with the FDIC (Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation), not from selling shares.
- **Berkshire Hathaway:** It sold about $30.7 billion of stocks in 2025, but the filing doesn't name any position it fully exited. It wrote down Kraft Heinz and Occidental but still owns both.
- **ExxonMobil:** Its 2025 sales were the Singapore retail fuels business, Mobil Argentina S.A., its French affiliates and some U.S. assets. Those are subsidiaries, businesses or assets, which you asked me to exclude.
- **Boeing:** It sold parts of its Digital Aviation Solutions business (Jeppesen, ForeFlight, AerData, OzRunways) to Thoma Bravo. That is a business, not an investment.

Two near-misses: Walmart also sold Alert Innovation in fiscal 2025, but that was a subsidiary. Pfizer's agreement to sell its ViiV stake was announced in January 2026, after its fiscal year ended.

I read the sections where these sales would normally appear: investment and fair-value notes, other income, divestitures and the MD&A (management's discussion and analysis). I didn't read every page, so I can't rule out a passing mention elsewhere.
